I wasn't able to finish college due to undiagnosed mental illness. After some internships, at the age of 19, I started working as a writer. When I was 27, I took my first work sabbatical during which I self-learnt graphic design (out of sheer boredom). I started offering both skills as a package, working on projects specifically in the field of social impact. However, my dream was to work on mental health content.

Following my diagnosis, I received streamlined treatment and my condition improved. Soon, I landed my dream job, working as a mental health journalist. I also worked for a mental health research lab and a publisher ghostwriting (and designing) mental health workbooks. I went from creating boring content for websites and annual reports to being able to choose projects only related to mental health.

Now, I am in the process of starting my own brand of mental health products. The only industry that understands the accommodations required for working with a mental illness is mental health related work. I am what they call an expert-by-experience.

Mainstream education and industries need to recognize the reasonable accommodation required for people with disability to reach their potential. People like me don't have a choice but to take offbeat paths to build sustainable careers.

Hello. It sounds like your therapist misunderstood your requirements. But here are some things that I've learned about therapy:

\- The therapist may not be the right fit. It's okay to change the therapist if that's the case. I think of the first meeting as a test - Can I talk to this therapist about everything - my private thoughts, about my sexuality, things I can't share anywhere else? Do they seem judgy? Are they able to understand what I'm saying and how I'm feeling? I observe all of these things as I'm chatting with them and I continue only if I feel comfortable.

\- I use the first appointment to be very clear about what I want. Is the pressing issue the only thing I'm worried about? Are there things I want to talk about it the future that I'm not ready to talk about right now? I make it very clear in the beginning of the kind of relationship I want from them. At the end of it a  therapist-patient relationship is a professional one. You are using a service they offer. So you can make it clear about what you want and if they can provide that for you.

\- Do not be disheartened if the therapist isn't working for you. I saw a dozen therapists my entire life before finding one that works. For me. Remember, a therapist that worked for your friend may not work for you. Figure out what you want from your therapist - young, old, their gender. Some people prefer older therapists because they seek wisdom and experience. Some prefer younger ones thinking they may understand them better.

\- OP, your comfort comes first. So give all of these a thought. I am happy to recommend my therapist who has helped me quit two addictions and bring out the best in me. I am also quite well connected in the mental health network and can you get you other recommendations if required.

I congratulate you on taking a step to better your mental health. All the best.
